interest: This file provides valuable empirical insight into the transnational movement and diplomatic surveillance of second-generation Japanese Americans (Nisei) during the escalating international tensions of the late 1930s. Consul Boyce's analysis is particularly noteworthy for directly confronting and debunking sensationalist press reports alleging that Japanese Americans were repatriating in large numbers due to domestic discrimination or to enlist in the Japanese imperial military following the 1937 outbreak of the Sino-Japanese War; consular statistics revealed instead a 30 percent decline in departures for Japan. The documents also demonstrate the routine interdepartmental intelligence coordination between the Department of State, the Department of Labor's Immigration and Naturalization Service, and naval authorities over travel documentation, dual citizenship concerns, and Pacific port movements on the eve of World War II.
overview: This file (894.5511) contains U.S. State Department correspondence and cross-references from December 1936 to March 1939 concerning immigration and travel between the United States and Japan. The file begins with a 1936 cross-reference sheet regarding Japanese passport requirements for naval personnel and passengers traveling to Guam via Yokohama on the USS Gold Star. The core of the file consists of a February 1939 despatch from American Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama examining travel patterns of second-generation Japanese Americans (Nisei) following the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War ('China Incident') in July 1937. Addressing press reports that anti-Japanese sentiment in the U.S. or militaristic enthusiasm was driving young Japanese Americans to repatriate, Boyce presents port data showing an actual 30 percent drop in travel to Japan between 1937 and 1938. The file concludes with Far Eastern Affairs division clearance and a formal request from the Secretary of State to the Secretary of Labor to obtain updated entry and departure figures from the Bureau of Immigration for Pacific Coast ports and Honolulu.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note concerning Japanese passport regulations for passengers on the naval supply ship USS Gold Star traveling to Guam.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Despatch No. 271 (filed under 138/3635) from Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama. It highlights that Japanese authorities will no longer permit passengers aboard the USS Gold Star, a naval supply ship for the unit at Guam, to land using certificates of identity issued by the Governor of Guam without a written consular guarantee. Boyce recommends that the Navy Department be advised to provide standard passports to all personnel dispatched to Guam to prevent travel disruptions.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 271 regarding passport requirements for USS Gold Star passengers

subfiles.about: Consular despatch reporting on the travel patterns of second-generation Japanese Americans and requesting updated entry and departure statistics.
subfiles.summary: Consul Richard F. Boyce reports from Yokohama on the situation of native-born Japanese Americans living in or traveling to Japan following the outbreak of the Sino-Japanese conflict in July 1937. In response to newspaper claims that rising numbers of Japanese Americans were returning to Japan due to racial prejudice in the U.S. or to join the Japanese armed forces, Boyce provides port statistics showing a 30 percent decrease in departures to Japan between fiscal years 1937 and 1938. He asks the Department of State to request that the Bureau of Immigration provide updated entry and departure statistics for Pacific Coast ports and Honolulu from July 1, 1938 onward to assist in monitoring the community.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 475 from Consul Richard F. Boyce on repatriation and travel of Americans of Japanese race

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum approving the consular request for Japanese American migration and travel statistics.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs indicates that the division has no objection to complying with the request made by Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama. The memorandum approves asking the Bureau of Immigration in Washington to supply the Yokohama consulate with entry and departure statistics for Americans of Japanese race through Pacific Coast ports and Honolulu. The memorandum is routed forward to the Visa Division for implementation.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Division of Far Eastern Affairs on travel statistics for Japanese Americans

subfiles.about: Official diplomatic communication requesting the Department of Labor to supply immigration statistics on Japanese American travelers.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State presents his compliments to the Secretary of Labor requesting that the Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization provide specific travel figures. The requested data includes entry and departure numbers for American citizens of the Japanese race at Pacific Coast ports and Honolulu covering the period from July 1, 1938 to date. This request carries out the statistical inquiry initiated by the American Consulate in Yokohama.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State to Secretary of Labor requesting immigration statistics
